sections.title: Verb + object + -ing or possessive + -ing
sections.content:
Some verbs can be followed either by an object + -ing or a possessive + -ing with a similar meaning, although the possessive + -ing form is usually considered to be rather formal:
• I resented Tom winning the prize. (more formally I resented Tom’s winning...)
• Mia recalled him buying the book. (more formally Mia recalled his buying...)
Also: detest, (dis)approve of, (dis)like, hate, love, object to (= ‘(dis)liking’ verbs); forget, imagine, remember, think of (= ‘thinking’ verbs)

sections.title: Verb + to + -ing
sections.content:
Some verbs can be followed by to + -ing where to is a preposition:
• She confessed to stealing the money.
• You don’t object to working late tonight, do you?
Also: adapt, adjust, admit, look forward, own up, resort

sections.title: Verb + preposition + -ing
sections.content:
Other verbs can be followed by different prepositions + -ing:
• by + -ing: Can you begin by cleaning the floors...? (also: close, end, finish, open, start)
• on + -ing (or on + object + -ing): Clare insisted on (Jack) wearing a suit... (also: concentrate, count, depend, focus, insist, rely)
• of + -ing (or of + object + -ing): Have you ever heard of (anyone) getting arrested...? (also: approve, hear, know, speak, talk, tell)
• object + from + -ing: The noise prevented me (from) sleeping. (also: deter, discourage, keep, prevent, prohibit, stop)

sections.title: Object + -ing or bare infinitive
sections.content:
Some verbs (feel, hear, notice, observe, overhear, see, watch) can be followed by an object and then either by an -ing form or bare infinitive, but the meanings may be slightly different:
• I saw them playing football... (-ing indicates an action in progress)
• I saw him smash the bottle. (bare infinitive indicates a completed action)

sections.title: Bare infinitive or to-infinitive
sections.content:
After the verbs dare and help we can use either a bare infinitive or to-infinitive:
• I didn’t dare (to) say anything.
• We hope the campaign will help (to) raise awareness...
After have, let and make we can use an object + bare infinitive but not to-infinitive:
• His exam results might make him work harder.

exercises.question: I really hate you having to be away from home so much. (Rewrite using possessive)
options: I really hate your having to be away...
I really hate you to be away...
I really hate you being away...
exercises.hint: Possessive form of the object before -ing.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I really hate your having to be away...
Possessive form of the object before -ing. This verb pattern requires a gerund (-ing form) as its object.

exercises.sentence: I really enjoy to swim in the open sea on hot summer days.
exercises.correction: I really enjoy swimming in the open sea on hot summer days.
exercises.hint: 'Enjoy' always takes a gerund (-ing), never a to-infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: enjoy swimming
'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund (-ing form), never a to-infinitive. Other verbs that take only the gerund: avoid, consider, deny, dislike, finish, imagine, involve, keep, mention, mind, miss, practise, risk, suggest. A useful test: if you can replace the verb with 'stop/continue', it usually takes a gerund.

exercises.question: I have always detested the dog jumping up at me. (Rewrite using possessive)
options: I have always detested the dog's jumping up at me.
I have always detested the dog jumping at me.
I have always detested how the dog jumps.
exercises.hint: Possessive form is possible with 'the dog'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I have always detested the dog's jumping up at me.
Possessive form is possible with 'the dog'. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: She avoided to mention the subject whenever her sister was present.
exercises.correction: She avoided mentioning the subject whenever her sister was present.
exercises.hint: 'Avoid' takes a gerund (-ing), never a to-infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: avoided mentioning
'Avoid' is always followed by a gerund. Using a to-infinitive ('avoided to mention') is incorrect in standard English. The gerund after 'avoid' indicates the action being prevented: 'avoid making', 'avoid saying', 'avoid going'.

exercises.question: In a survey, 65% of dentists said that they had made mistakes... (Rewrite with 'owned up')
exercises.explanation:
Answer: ...owned up to making mistakes.
Own up + to + -ing. This verb pattern requires a gerund (-ing form) as its object.

exercises.question: Do you fancy ___ (go) for a walk along the river this afternoon?
exercises.explanation:
Answer: going
'Fancy' (informal British English for 'want' or 'feel like') always takes a gerund: fancy going, fancy doing, fancy having. It never takes a to-infinitive. Other verbs that follow the same pattern: feel like, can't help, can't stand, look forward to.

exercises.question: I heard the tyre ___ and then the lorry skidded across the road.
exercises.hint: Both are possible, but 'burst' might suggest the completed sound of the pop.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: burst / bursting
Both are possible, but 'burst' might suggest the completed sound of the pop.

exercises.question: She felt the wasp ___ her just before she brushed it off her arm.
exercises.hint: Both -ing and bare infinitive are possible with 'feel'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both are possible
Both -ing and bare infinitive are possible with 'feel'. This verb pattern requires a gerund (-ing form) as its object.

exercises.question: We didn't agree with the decision, but we didn't dare ___ protest against it.
exercises.hint: Dare can take bare or to-infinitive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: (to)
Dare can take bare or to-infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.

exercises.question: The dial on the left lets ___ control the speed of the fan.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: you
Let + object + bare infinitive. This verb pattern requires a to-infinitive as its complement.
